chapters.title: Chapter 2: What You Give Up and What You Keep

lessons.title: What Works in Both Regimes: Standard Deduction, Employer NPS and More

children.text: The last two lessons were a list of losses. This one is the list of what you keep. It is shorter, but it is not trivial. Some of it is bigger in the new regime than in the old one, and one item, employer NPS, is the single most useful tax lever left for a salaried person who has moved to the new regime.

body.text: The new regime takes away deductions for how you spend and invest. It does not take away the tax-free treatment of most money you receive when you retire, leave a job or reinvest capital gains.

children.text: 1. Standard Deduction: Bigger in the New Regime

body.caption: Flat Deductions for Salary and Pension Income

cells: Family members receiving pension after an employee's death

body.text: The new regime starts every salaried person ₹25,000 ahead on standard deduction. When you compare regimes, remember to use ₹75,000 on the new side and ₹50,000 on the old side. Using the same number for both is one of the most common calculation errors.

children.text: 2. Employer NPS: The Best Lever Left

markDefs.definition: Reorganising the components of your cost to company, for example moving part of a special allowance into an employer NPS contribution, without changing the total CTC.

children.text: Your employer's contribution to your NPS account is deductible under Section 124 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 80CCD(2) of the 1961 Act) in both regimes. In the new regime the limit is 14% of basic plus DA. In the old regime it is 10% for private sector employees. Many companies offer this through
, usually once a year during the benefits window.

body.caption: New regime version. Karan in Gurugram has basic salary of ₹12,00,000 a year and is in the 30% slab: 14% × ₹12,00,000 = ₹1,68,000, and ₹1,68,000 × 30% × 1.04 = ₹52,416 of tax saved every year.

body.title: Value of Employer NPS
body.prompt: Divya is a senior manager at a Chennai logistics company, in the new regime and the 30% slab. Her basic salary is ₹80,000 a month with no DA. If her employer contributes the full 14% of basic to NPS, how much tax does she save in a year, including 4% cess? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: Annual basic is ₹9,60,000. 14% of that is ₹1,34,400. Tax saved is ₹1,34,400 × 30% × 1.04, which is ₹41,932.80, or about ₹41,933.

body.text: Three catches before you sign up. First, restructuring is CTC-neutral, so your monthly take-home falls by the amount moved to NPS. Second, the money is largely locked until 60. Third, employer contributions to EPF, NPS and superannuation above ₹7.5 lakh a year in total are taxed as a perquisite, which matters for very high earners.

body.title: Lock In the Limit
body.textWithBlank: In the new regime, your employer's NPS contribution is deductible up to ___% of basic salary plus DA.
body.explanation: The new regime allows 14%. The old regime allows 10% for private sector employees and 14% for government employees.

children.text: 3. Money That Stays Tax-Free in Both Regimes

The new regime removed a specific list of exemptions: HRA, LTA, most allowances, professional tax and the like. Everything outside that list keeps working as before. Most of it relates to leaving a job or retiring, which is exactly when the amounts get large.

body.title: Ramesh Iyer's Retirement Year
body.scenario: Ramesh Iyer turns 60 and retires from a private textile company in Coimbatore in June 2026. In tax year 2026-27 he receives ₹4,50,000 of salary for April to June, ₹14,00,000 of gratuity, ₹6,00,000 of leave encashment and ₹3,00,000 of FD interest. He pays a ₹40,000 health insurance premium. His son believes the huge gratuity will push him into the 30% slab and that the old regime, with its senior citizen benefits, must be better.
body.prompt: Is his son right? Which regime should Ramesh pick?
body.modelAnswer: No. Gratuity of ₹14 lakh is within the ₹20 lakh limit and leave encashment of ₹6 lakh is within ₹25 lakh, and both exemptions apply in either regime, so neither amount is taxed at all. His taxable income comes only from salary and FD interest, ₹7,50,000 in total. In the new regime, subtracting the ₹75,000 standard deduction leaves ₹6,75,000, below the ₹12 lakh rebate limit, so his tax is nil. In the old regime he gets the ₹50,000 standard deduction, up to ₹50,000 on FD interest under 80TTB for senior citizens, and ₹40,000 under 80D, leaving ₹6,10,000. Senior citizen slabs give tax of ₹10,000 plus 20% of ₹1,10,000 (₹22,000), which is ₹32,000, plus ₹1,280 cess, a total of ₹33,280. The new regime wins by ₹33,280.

children.text: The new regime removes allowances that are really extra pay, like HRA or children's education allowance. It keeps exemptions for money that covers the cost of doing your job. Genuine reimbursement of official expenses, backed by bills, is not your income in the first place.

body.title: Which One Survives?
body.question: Ishaan, a new regime taxpayer, is a field sales executive at an FMCG company in Ahmedabad. Which of these receipts remains exempt in his hands?
options: ₹1,20,000 of HRA, since he pays rent
₹30,000 of LTA used for a family trip to Goa
₹45,000 of daily allowance paid while travelling to distributors across Gujarat
₹2,500 of professional tax deducted from his salary
body.explanation: Daily allowance for official tours covers the cost of doing his job and stays exempt in the new regime. HRA and LTA are among the exemptions the new regime removes, and professional tax is not deductible in the new regime.

children.text: 5. Capital Gains Exemptions and a Few Others

Investors keep all the capital gains relief. The first ₹1.25 lakh of long-term gains on listed shares and equity mutual funds each year is untaxed in both regimes. Reinvestment exemptions under Sections 54, 54EC and 54F of the 1961 Act, which let you save tax on long-term gains by buying a house or specified bonds, work in both regimes too. So does the Agniveer Corpus Fund deduction under Section 80CCH.

body.text: Some smaller deductions do not survive and are easy to forget. Savings account interest under 80TTA (₹10,000), senior citizen deposit interest under 80TTB (₹50,000), education loan interest under 80E and donations under 80G are all old regime only. If you give heavily to eligible charities or are repaying a large education loan, count them in your comparison.

body.title: Squeeze the Most Out of the New Regime
steps: Ask HR whether your company offers employer NPS under 80CCD(2) and when the restructuring window opens
Calculate 14% of your basic plus DA and the tax it would save at your slab
Check that your take-home pay still covers your monthly budget after restructuring
Make sure official travel and phone costs are claimed as bill-backed reimbursements, not paid as taxable allowances
If you are planning to sell a property or shares, note that capital gains exemptions work in either regime

points: The standard deduction survives and is larger in the new regime: ₹75,000 against ₹50,000.
Employer NPS under Section 124 (80CCD(2)) is allowed up to 14% of basic plus DA in the new regime, making it the best remaining lever for salaried taxpayers.
Retirement and exit receipts such as gratuity, leave encashment, commuted pension and EPF withdrawals keep their exemptions in both regimes.
Official allowances and bill-backed reimbursements stay exempt. Allowances that are really extra pay, like HRA and LTA, do not.
Capital gains exemptions, including the ₹1.25 lakh equity LTCG exemption and reinvestment under Sections 54, 54EC and 54F, work in both regimes.
80TTA, 80TTB, 80E and 80G are old regime only, so include them when you compare.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Rules reflect tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing. Several provisions are cited by their Income-tax Act, 1961 references and should be confirmed against the corresponding sections of the Income-tax Act, 2025. Consult a qualified tax professional before filing.
